source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC paper)
finding: CompressARC is a small network with random start. It trains on one puzzle at test time. The loss is code length: KL of a latent plus reconstruction of the demo grids. It never sees the held-out answer.
numbers: 76K parameters. 2000 Adam steps per puzzle (lr 0.01, betas 0.5/0.9), about 20 min per puzzle on one RTX 4070. Solves 34.75% of the 400 ARC-1 training puzzles and 20% of the 400 evaluation puzzles (pass@2).
quote: Despite never using the training set, performing no pretraining, and having only 76K parameters
limits: Alternative solver, not an LLM. Research code on public sets; ARC-AGI-1 only.
agent_relevance: A per-task learner whose only signal is how short the description gets. Compare with our G3 rule: pass on something not fitted.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC paper)
finding: Accuracy rises with inference compute and keeps rising to 2000 steps. Training set, pass@2 by step: 100 steps 2.25%, 300 21.25%, 500 27.5%, 1000 31.75%, 2000 34.75%.
numbers: Train pass@1 at 2000 steps 30.25%, pass@10 41.5%, pass@100 48.5%, pass@1000 52.75% (Table 4). Time 130 h total for 400 puzzles.
limits: Many samples from many runs reach 52.75%; official score needs 2 guesses only.
agent_relevance: Shows a long tail of useful extra compute per task; the gap pass@2 vs pass@1000 (about 18 points) is the room a better selector could use.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC paper)
finding: Same curve on the evaluation set. Pass@2 by step: 100 steps 1.25%, 300 10.75%, 500 15%, 1000 19.25%, 1500 21.5%, 2000 20%.
numbers: Eval pass@1 18.5%, pass@10 26%, pass@100 31.25%, pass@1000 33.75% at 2000 steps (Table 5). 138 h total.
limits: Pass@2 dips from 21.5% (1500 steps) to 20% (2000) while pass@1 still rises, so late-step selection is noisy.
agent_relevance: Stopping and answer selection are separate problems; more compute does not always raise the 2-guess score.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC paper)
finding: Answer choice: sample the decoder output throughout training, then pick the most frequent answers. The blog adds an exponential moving average (decay 0.97) and downweighting of uncertain samples.
numbers: Details in method section; blog gives EMA decay 0.97.
limits: No ablation table isolating the selection rule.
agent_relevance: Same idea as voting over attempts. Our G4 warns that agreement is a hint, not proof.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC paper)
finding: Compression is the stated mechanism: fewer bits to describe the puzzle correlates with a more accurate solution. The authors frame this as finding a short program that outputs the puzzle set.
numbers: The loss ignores the held-out output grid; the answer comes from the decoder, not from a separate search.
quote: A more efficient (i.e., lower-bit) compression of a puzzle correlates with a more accurate solution.
limits: The link between bits and correctness is shown by case studies, not by a measured correlation across all puzzles in the text read.
agent_relevance: Candidate selector for our agent: among programs that all fit the examples, prefer the shortest. Needs a real test on our items.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC paper)
finding: Hand-built inductive biases do the work. Network is symmetric to example order, colour permutation and rotation/reflection. Special layers give specific skills. Authors say the abilities come from layers they designed for that purpose.
numbers: Abilities seen: colour-to-procedure, infilling, cropping, connecting dots (including 45 degree lines), same-colour detection, pixel adjacency, short translation.
limits: Skills are listed from examples, not scored per category.
agent_relevance: Compression only finds short codes in the language it is given. Our scaffold's operators O1-O8 play the role of that language.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC paper)
finding: Failure list. It cannot do: assign two colours to each other, repeat an operation serially, count, translate/rotate/rescale/duplicate at scale, detect connectivity, plan or simulate agents, extend patterns over long range.
numbers: Examples named: 0d3d703e, 0a938d79, ce9e57f2, 7b6016b9, 2dd70a9a, 28e73c20.
limits: Qualitative; no count of how many of the 800 puzzles fall in each class.
agent_relevance: Marks the boundary of the method: short code in a weak language fails on counting and long-range rules. Route such tasks to other solvers.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC paper)
finding: Reconstruction-only training can settle on memorisation. In the Bounding Box puzzle, information about light blue pixels moved out of the latent into the nonlinear layers, with no change in output.
numbers: Tensor [example,height,width,channel] lost most of its information between steps 600 and 1000 (puzzle 6d75e8bb).
limits: One case study.
agent_relevance: A short code in the latent can be fake: the answer may be stored elsewhere. Shows code length depends on what you count as the code.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC paper)
finding: Failed or weak ideas, all reported: hierarchical decoding (first layer absorbs the KL), convolution-like copy layers (noise), tropical convolution (works on toy puzzles only), KL floor against collapse (never saw recovery), joint training across puzzles (not tried).
numbers: Appendix K. No numbers for the failed variants.
limits: Negative results are stated qualitatively only.
agent_relevance: Do not assume the clean compression story; the working system needed many ARC-specific fixes.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC paper)
finding: Baseline comparison. A U-Net trained only on the target puzzle's demo pairs, same no-pretraining rule, was built to match CompressARC. In the appendix it is described as solving 2.5% of the training set without augmentation and 1% with augmentation.
numbers: U-Net: 10000 steps; shape-mismatch puzzles scored zero. Main Table 1 also lists a U-Net row, but its text was garbled in extraction, so the two figures may not describe the same run; exact Table 1 values not recorded.
limits: Weak baseline by the authors' own choice; figures need a recheck against the PDF table.
agent_relevance: Control that the gain is the compression objective plus architecture, not just per-task training.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) CompressARC blog post
finding: Blog gives the same results and details of the run. Per-puzzle model is fresh; one model, one puzzle, one answer. Reconstruction loss is weighted heavily (10x) against KL.
numbers: Pass@2 34.75% train, 20% eval; 20 min per puzzle, RTX 4070.
limits: Same authors as the paper; no independent run.
agent_relevance: Confirms the paper numbers on a second page.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) CompressARC blog post
finding: Seed fragility. In replications of Color the Boxes, one of four necessary latent tensors sometimes fell to zero information, and then CompressARC typically did not recover the right answer.
numbers: Puzzle 272f95fa; solved in about 150 steps in the shown run.
quote: In some replications... one of these four necessary tensors fall to zero information content
limits: Blog says which tensors survive varies across runs. No rate given.
agent_relevance: Run-to-run variance is real; one run is not evidence. Matches our G4 on correlated and unstable samples.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) CompressARC blog post
finding: Regularisation on network weights is derived but not used. Authors say they do not know if it matters.
numbers: Statement in blog: not used.
quote: We don't use it. Maybe it matters, but we don't know.
limits: Open question.
agent_relevance: Code length of the model itself is left out; pure data-fit plus latent cost only. A partial MDL.

source: ARC Prize Foundation (2025) ARC Prize 2025 results and analysis
finding: Official recognition and the ARC-AGI-2 result. CompressARC took 3rd paper award ($5k). Reported as about 20-34% on ARC-AGI-1 and about 4% on ARC-AGI-2.
numbers: Paper awards: 1st Tiny Recursive Model ($50k), 2nd Pourcel/Colas/Oudeyer ($20k), 3rd Liao and Gu ($5k). Page names zero-pretraining as one of three 2025 themes.
limits: The ~4% ARC-AGI-2 figure is the page's summary; I did not find the source run.
agent_relevance: On the harder successor benchmark per-task compression is near the floor; do not expect it to carry hard items.

source: ARC Prize Foundation (2025) ARC Prize 2025 results and analysis
finding: Context for what wins. Kaggle ARC-AGI-2 private top was 24.03% (NVARC), 16.53% (ARChitects), 12.64% (MindsAI). The page says the central 2025 theme is refinement loops and test-time adaptation.
numbers: 1,455 teams, 15,154 entries. Poetiq refinement on Gemini 3 Pro 54% at about $30/task; Gemini 3 Pro base 31% at $0.81; Claude Opus 4.5 Thinking 64k 37.6% at $2.20.
limits: Verified commercial numbers from the page; costs approximate.
agent_relevance: The strongest 2025 systems loop on real feedback (our G2), not on code length. Compression is a side route.

source: Jolicoeur-Martineau (2025) Less is More: Recursive Reasoning with Tiny Networks (TRM)
finding: Tiny network trained on ARC data with heavy augmentation. Beats CompressARC's no-pretraining level by a wide margin on ARC-AGI-1, but uses training data.
numbers: TRM-Att 7M params: ARC-1 44.6%, ARC-2 7.8% (2 tries). HRM 27M: 40.3% and 5.0%. Direct-prediction transformer 27M: 21.0% and 0.0%. Voting over 1000 augmentations at test time.
limits: Trained on ARC training set plus 160 extra tasks; not zero-pretraining. Different regime from CompressARC.
agent_relevance: Gives the ceiling for small non-LLM solvers with data; CompressARC's 20% is the zero-data point on the same axis.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Hierarchical Reasoning Model
finding: HRM paper itself compares to CompressARC: its plain Direct-prediction transformer baseline matches Liao and Gu on ARC-1. Swapping in the hierarchical design plus adaptive halting gave more than twofold gain.
numbers: HRM ARC-AGI-1 40.3%, ARC-AGI-2 5%, vs o3-mini-high 34.5%. Extra inference compute gave minimal gains on ARC.
quote: Direct pred matches the performance of Liao and Gu
limits: Paper reports Direct pred 21.0% (via TRM Table 5); text says it matches Liao and Gu (about 20%).
agent_relevance: Shows a plain per-task-trained transformer equals CompressARC's score; the compression objective is not clearly the cause.

source: ARC Prize Team (2025) The Hidden Drivers of HRM's Performance on ARC-AGI
finding: Independent audit of HRM on hidden data. The score fell and the architecture mattered less than claimed.
numbers: ARC-AGI-1 semi-private 32% (vs 41% claimed on public eval); ARC-AGI-2 2%. Cost $1.48 per task (ARC-1), $1.68 (ARC-2).
limits: Run on the foundation's hidden sets; one team.
agent_relevance: A replication check on the pattern: claimed small-model gains shrink on held-out data.

source: ARC Prize Team (2025) The Hidden Drivers of HRM's Performance on ARC-AGI
finding: Where HRM's gain comes from: the outer refinement loop and training on the evaluation tasks, not the H/L architecture.
numbers: 1 to 2 loops: +13 points. Training on 400 eval tasks only: 31% pass@2 vs 41% full mix. About 300 train augmentations reach near max; 30 are within 4%. A plain 27M transformer is within ~5 points of HRM.
limits: Ablations by the ARC Prize team, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Test-time learning on each task plus augmentation carries most of the effect; code length is one way to drive it, not the only one.

source: ARC Prize Team (2025) The Hidden Drivers of HRM's Performance on ARC-AGI
finding: The team calls HRM a zero-pretraining test-time-training method and guesses a per-task run would match CompressARC's 21% pass@2, but says they did not test it.
numbers: Stated as a hypothesis; no number measured.
limits: Untested speculation.
agent_relevance: Weak link between CompressARC and HRM; treat as open.

source: Franzen, Disselhoff, Hartmann (2025) Product of Experts with LLMs: Boosting Performance on ARC Is a Matter of Perspective
finding: An LLM scores candidate answers by the product of its probabilities under 16 re-augmented views of the task. This is a description-length-style score (negative log likelihood summed over views) used to pick answers.
numbers: ARC public eval 2-guess: NeMo-Minitron-8B baseline 18.3%, +TTT 44.5%, +16xAug 62.5%, +PoE 67.6%, +DFS 71.6%. Llama-3.2-3B: 14.9, 40.9, 52.9, 59.5, 61.4. Final 71.6% (286.5/400).
limits: Public eval, with fine-tuning on RE-ARC and per-task TTT; score by authors.
agent_relevance: A concrete code-length-like selector in an LLM loop: it adds 5.1 points over picking by single-view probability for the 8B model. Worth copying for answer choice.

source: Franzen, Disselhoff, Hartmann (2025) Product of Experts with LLMs
finding: Cost of per-task training is small. DFS sampling at T=9% finds 76.0% of correct candidates against 77.3% for 4x stochastic sampling but uses a quarter of the time and half the false positives.
numbers: Initial fine-tune 98 H100 GPU hours; test-time training about 51 s per task on an RTX 4090. DFS 9:32h vs 39:47h for stochastic.
limits: Single hardware setup.
agent_relevance: Per-task adaptation of an LLM costs about a minute, versus 20 minutes for CompressARC from scratch.

source: Akyurek et al. (2024) The Surprising Effectiveness of Test-Time Training for Few-Shot Learning
finding: Test-time training with a LoRA adapter per task on leave-one-out copies of the demo pairs lifts a fine-tuned 8B model. Per-task adapters beat a shared one.
numbers: ARC (80-task subset, pass@2): up to 6x over fine-tuned baseline; 53.0% on public validation with 8B model, 61.9% with program-synthesis ensemble. BIG-Bench Hard 10-shot 50.5% to 57.8% (+7.3). Per-task LoRA beat shared by 7 tasks (24%).
limits: Already covered in 08 evidence; included for the contrast with compression-driven training.
agent_relevance: Both adapt weights per puzzle; TTT uses a prediction loss on demos, CompressARC a code-length loss. Same family, no head-to-head.

source: Pourcel, Colas, Oudeyer (2026) SOAR: Self-Improving Language Models for Evolutionary Program Synthesis
finding: LLM writes Python programs, refines them using execution feedback, and is fine-tuned on its own search traces. This is a search loop over programs checked by running them, not a compression loop.
numbers: ARC test: 52% with all models and majority voting (oracle 57.25%). 14B model 36.25% at 6k budget with SOAR vs 14.25% Sample&Refine. One-shot Claude-4-Sonnet 20.75%, GPT-4.1 8.00%, o3-mini 38.25%.
limits: Search budget 3k samples + 3k refinements per task.
agent_relevance: A working agent loop with real feedback; shows what the strong alternative to MDL selection looks like.

source: Hu et al. (2025) ARC Is a Vision Problem! (VARC)
finding: A vision transformer trained on ARC data plus test-time training per task. Cites CompressARC and says some tasks can be solved from scratch.
numbers: ARC-1 pass@2: 54.5% (18M ViT), 60.4% ensemble. TTT with no offline training: 26.4%. TTT per task beat joint TTT on all test tasks by about 10 points.
quote: some tasks in this benchmark can be solved tabula rasa
limits: Trained on ARC-1 training set; ARC-2 models trained on ARC-1.
agent_relevance: Independent number for 'no offline training' per-task learning: 26.4%, above CompressARC's 20%. Per-task isolation matters.

source: Sun et al. (2020) Test-Time Training with Self-Supervision for Generalization under Distribution Shifts
finding: Founding test-time training paper: update the model on a self-supervised loss from a single test sample before predicting.
numbers: Task is rotation prediction. TTT often improves over joint training by more than 10% on CIFAR-10-C level 5 and never hurt by more than 0.2%; TTT-Online gave over 24% on three noise types.
limits: Image classification, not LLM; figures read from text, not rechecked against tables.
agent_relevance: Origin of per-instance adaptation at inference. CompressARC swaps the proxy loss for code length.

source: Hardt and Sun (2024) Test-Time Training on Nearest Neighbors for Large Language Models
finding: Fine-tune a language model at test time on retrieved neighbours of each input. Gains come in bits per byte, which is code length.
numbers: About 20 neighbours and one gradient step each cut bits per byte by 20% on Pile tasks; larger drop on code (pile github). Narrows gap between small GPT-2 and GPT-Neo over 10x larger.
limits: Needs a large embedding index of Pile; sufficient index quality and size are necessary.
agent_relevance: Language-model cost measured in bits is lowered by test-time updates; supports the code-length view for text agents.

source: Chollet et al. (2025) ARC Prize 2024 Technical Report
finding: Test-time training was the key 2024 technique. ARChitects used it for first place; MindsAI pioneered it from 2023.
numbers: Private-eval top: ARChitects 53.5%, MindsAI 55.5% (not eligible for prize), Icecuber brute-force 20% in 2020. 2024 SOTA rose from 33% to 55.5%.
limits: Report predates CompressARC, which it does not mention.
agent_relevance: Per-task weight updates at inference are now standard; compression is one way to define the loss.

source: Liao and Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining
finding: Gap note. I found no independent replication, no LLM-agent-loop version, and no 2026 follow-up of CompressARC in the sources reachable this session. The citing papers (HRM, VARC) refer to it only as a baseline.
numbers: Search tools hit rate limits (Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, web search budget); coverage of citations is incomplete.
limits: Absence of evidence under a limited search, not proof of none.
agent_relevance: Treat CompressARC as a single-source result [S] in the schema until tested on our items.
